source: Round 5 (gc5): GC trade knowledge (IRC/IBC 2021 residential and commercial details, concrete, masonry, roofing, drywall, plan reading, estimating) and national business & law (bonds, liens, AIA, labor, payroll tax, depreciation, ratios, OSHA recordkeeping, EEO)

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, a stairway must be at least 36 in clear width above the handrail height. Handrails may stick out no more than 4-1/2 in on each side, so the clear width at and below the handrail must be at least 31-1/2 in with one handrail and 27 in with handrails on both sides.
facts.note: Confirmed against the 2021 IRC text reproduced in Viewrail's 2021 IRC visual interpretation and a California (CRC) building department handout.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, one flight of stairs may not rise more than 12 ft 7 in (151 in) vertically between floor levels or landings. A taller rise needs an intermediate landing.
facts.note: Confirmed by Viewrail's reproduction of the 2021 IRC text and Montana DLI 2021 IRC means of egress training.

facts.fact: In a dwelling stairway (2021 IRC), the tallest riser in a flight may be no more than 3/8 in taller than the shortest riser, and the deepest tread may be no more than 3/8 in deeper than the shallowest tread.
facts.note: Confirmed by Viewrail 2021 IRC reproduction, Montana DLI 2021 IRC training and a CRC handout.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, stairs with solid risers need a nosing projection of at least 3/4 in and no more than 1-1/4 in, with a nosing radius no larger than 9/16 in. A nosing is not required where the tread depth is at least 11 in.
facts.note: Confirmed by Viewrail 2021 IRC reproduction, Montana DLI 2021 IRC training and a CRC handout.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, winder treads must be at least 10 in deep measured at the walkline, which is 12 in from the narrow side of the turn, and at least 6 in deep at any point within the clear width of the stair.
facts.note: Confirmed by Viewrail 2021 IRC reproduction and Montana DLI 2021 IRC training.

facts.fact: Open risers are allowed in IRC stairways, but where the stair is more than 30 in above the floor or grade below, the openings between treads must not let a 4-in sphere pass through.
facts.note: Confirmed by Viewrail 2021 IRC reproduction, Montana DLI training and a CRC handout.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, every stairway needs a floor or landing at the top and bottom. A landing must be at least as wide as the stair it serves, and on a straight run it must be at least 36 in deep in the direction of travel.
facts.note: Confirmed by Viewrail 2021 IRC reproduction and Montana DLI training.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, a handrail is required on at least one side of each flight of stairs with four or more risers, and it must be continuous for the full length of the flight (limited interruptions are allowed at newel posts, landings and the lowest tread).
facts.note: Confirmed by Viewrail 2021 IRC reproduction and Montana DLI training.

facts.fact: IRC spiral stairs need a clear width of at least 26 in at and below the handrail, treads at least 6-3/4 in deep at the walkline (walkline radius no more than 24-1/2 in), identical treads, risers no taller than 9-1/2 in, and headroom of at least 6 ft 6 in.
facts.note: Width, tread, radius and headroom confirmed in Viewrail's 2021 IRC reproduction; 9-1/2 in riser and 26 in width confirmed in Montana DLI 2021 IRC training.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, guards are required on open sides of floors, stairs, ramps and landings that are more than 30 in above the floor or grade below, measured at any point within 36 in horizontally of the edge. Insect screening does not count as a guard.
facts.note: Confirmed by Viewrail 2021 IRC reproduction and Montana DLI training.

facts.fact: Required guards under the 2021 IRC must be at least 36 in high above the walking surface. Guards on the open sides of stairs must be at least 34 in high measured from the line of the nosings, and where the top of a stair guard also serves as the handrail it must be 34 to 38 in high.
facts.note: Confirmed by Viewrail 2021 IRC reproduction. Some states amend this (California requires 42 in).

facts.fact: IRC guards may not have openings that let a 4-in sphere pass. Two exceptions: the triangle formed by a stair riser, tread and bottom rail may not pass a 6-in sphere, and guards on the open side of stairs may not pass a 4-3/8-in sphere.
facts.note: Confirmed by Viewrail 2021 IRC reproduction, Montana DLI training and a CRC handout.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, an operable window needs fall protection when its sill is less than 24 in above the finished floor and the opening is more than 72 in above the grade outside. The window must either not open far enough to pass a 4-in sphere or have an ASTM F2090 opening control or fall prevention device, and a required escape window must still give its full escape opening once the device is released.
facts.note: Confirmed by a 2021 IRC-based building department tip sheet (MyBuildingPermit TS 23).

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, basements, habitable attics and every sleeping room need at least one operable emergency escape and rescue opening, and a basement with sleeping rooms needs one in each sleeping room. Basements used only to house mechanical equipment and not over 200 sq ft are exempt.
facts.note: Confirmed by Boulder County (2021 IRC) and City of Boise building handouts.

facts.fact: IRC emergency escape and rescue openings need a net clear opening of at least 5.7 sq ft (5 sq ft is allowed for grade-floor openings), a net clear opening height of at least 24 in and a net clear width of at least 20 in. Because 24 x 20 in is only 3.3 sq ft, an opening at both minimum dimensions does not meet the area rule.
facts.note: Confirmed by Boulder County (2021 IRC) and Boise handouts. The 2018 IRC put all three numbers in R310.2.1; the 2021 IRC split the dimensions into R310.2.2.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, a window well serving an escape opening must have a horizontal area of at least 9 sq ft with a projection and width of at least 36 in. A well deeper than 44 in needs a permanently attached ladder or steps; ladder rungs must be at least 12 in wide inside, project at least 3 in from the wall and be spaced no more than 18 in apart vertically.
facts.note: Confirmed by Boulder County (2021 IRC numbering R310.4-R310.4.2.1) and Boise (2018 numbering R310.2.3) handouts. The ladder or steps may encroach up to 6 in into the required well size.

facts.fact: An emergency escape opening may open under a deck, porch or cantilever only if the window can open fully and there is a path at least 36 in high to a yard or court.
facts.note: Confirmed by Boise and Boulder County handouts.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, glazing in the fixed and operable panels of swinging, sliding and bifold doors is a hazardous location that needs safety glazing. Exceptions include openings that will not pass a 3-in sphere and decorative glazing.
facts.note: Confirmed by a 2021 IRC building department tip sheet (MyBuildingPermit TS 19).

facts.fact: Glazing next to a door needs safety glazing when its bottom edge is less than 60 in above the walking surface and it is within 24 in of either side of the door in the closed position. It is not required where a wall or permanent barrier separates the door and the glass.
facts.note: Confirmed by a 2021 IRC building department tip sheet (MyBuildingPermit TS 19).

facts.fact: A window pane needs safety glazing under the IRC only when all four conditions are met: it is larger than 9 sq ft, its bottom edge is less than 18 in above the floor, its top edge is more than 36 in above the floor, and a walking surface is within 36 in horizontally. A protective bar 34 to 38 in high that resists 50 lb per linear foot is an alternative.
facts.note: Confirmed by a 2021 IRC building department tip sheet (MyBuildingPermit TS 19).

facts.fact: Glazing in walls, enclosures or fences around tubs, showers, hot tubs, spas, saunas, steam rooms and pools needs safety glazing when its bottom edge is less than 60 in above the standing or walking surface. Glass more than 60 in horizontally from the water's edge is exempt.
facts.note: Confirmed by a 2021 IRC building department tip sheet (MyBuildingPermit TS 19).

facts.fact: Glazing beside stairs, ramps and landings needs safety glazing when its bottom edge is less than 36 in above the walking surface (unless it is more than 36 in away horizontally). At the bottom of a stair, glazing less than 36 in above the landing and within a 60-in horizontal arc of the bottom tread also needs safety glazing.
facts.note: Confirmed by a 2021 IRC building department tip sheet (MyBuildingPermit TS 19).

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, smoke alarms are required in each sleeping room, outside each separate sleeping area near the bedrooms, and on each additional story including basements and habitable attics (but not crawl spaces or uninhabitable attics).
facts.note: Confirmed by City of Boise and 2021 IRC (MyBuildingPermit TS 04) handouts.

facts.fact: Smoke alarms in dwellings must be kept back from permanently installed cooking appliances: at least 20 ft for ionization alarms, 10 ft for ionization alarms with a silencing switch, and 6 ft for photoelectric alarms, unless that would prevent a required location.
facts.note: Confirmed by City of Boise IRC handout and a 2021 IRC tip sheet that cites NFPA 72-2019.

facts.fact: When more than one smoke alarm is required in a dwelling unit, they must be interconnected so that one alarm sounding sets off all of them. Listed wireless interconnection is acceptable.
facts.note: Confirmed by City of Boise and 2021 IRC (MyBuildingPermit TS 04) handouts.

facts.fact: When permitted alterations, repairs or additions are made to an existing home, the house must get smoke alarms (and CO alarms where required) like a new dwelling. Work limited to exterior surfaces such as roofing, siding, windows or doors, or to plumbing or mechanical systems, is exempt.
facts.note: Confirmed by City of Boise and 2021 IRC (MyBuildingPermit TS 04) handouts.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, new dwellings need carbon monoxide alarms when they have a fuel-fired appliance or an attached garage with an opening into the home. The alarm goes outside each separate sleeping area near the bedrooms, and also inside a bedroom when a fuel-burning appliance is in that bedroom or its attached bathroom.
facts.note: Confirmed by City of Boise and 2021 IRC (MyBuildingPermit TS 04) handouts.

facts.fact: Under the IRC, a garage may not open directly into a room used for sleeping. Other doors between the garage and the house must be solid wood or solid or honeycomb-core steel at least 1-3/8 in thick, or 20-minute fire-rated, and have a self-closing or automatic-closing device.
facts.note: Confirmed by City of Boise and 2021 IRC (MyBuildingPermit TS 06) handouts.

facts.fact: Ducts in a garage, and ducts that pass through the walls or ceiling separating the house from the garage, must be at least No. 26 gage sheet steel (or other approved material) and may not have openings into the garage.
facts.note: Confirmed by City of Boise and 2021 IRC (MyBuildingPermit TS 06) handouts.

facts.fact: IRC garage separation: at least 1/2-in gypsum board on the garage side between the garage and the house and its attic; at least 5/8-in Type X gypsum board between the garage and habitable rooms above it; and at least 1/2-in gypsum board on structure that supports the separating floor/ceiling assembly.
facts.note: Confirmed by City of Boise and 2021 IRC (MyBuildingPermit TS 06) handouts.

facts.fact: For homes without sprinklers (2021 IRC), an exterior wall with a fire separation distance of less than 5 ft must be 1-hour fire-resistance rated with exposure from both sides; at 5 ft or more no rating is required. Projections such as eaves are not allowed closer than 2 ft and need 1-hour protection on the underside from 2 ft to under 5 ft.
facts.note: Confirmed by Pierce County WA 2021 code bulletin and the Michigan Residential Code table (Mich. Admin. Code R 408.30544b). Table footnotes allow some alternatives for projections (such as heavy timber or fire-retardant-treated wood); check the adopted table.

facts.fact: For homes without sprinklers (2021 IRC), wall openings such as windows and doors are not allowed where the fire separation distance is less than 3 ft, are limited to 25 percent of the wall area from 3 ft to under 5 ft, and are unlimited at 5 ft or more. Penetrations closer than 3 ft must be protected per R302.4.
facts.note: Confirmed by Pierce County WA 2021 code bulletin and the Michigan Residential Code table.

facts.fact: IRC concrete and masonry footings must be at least 12 in wide and 6 in thick (larger where Tables R403.1(1)-(3) require). The footing must project at least 2 in beyond the face of the foundation wall but not more than the footing's thickness.
facts.note: Confirmed by a 2021 IRC footing and foundation inspection guide (MyBuildingPermit).

facts.fact: IRC minimum concrete strengths: 2,500 psi for basement walls, foundations and interior slabs not exposed to weather; up to 3,000 psi for walls exposed to weather; and up to 3,500 psi for porches, steps and garage floor slabs in severe weathering areas. Exposed concrete in moderate and severe weathering areas must be air-entrained to 5-7 percent.
facts.note: Table text confirmed in a Penn State PHRC handout (2009 IRC) and the 3,000 psi / 5-7% air row confirmed in a 2021 IRC inspection guide; the table has not changed in later editions.

facts.fact: IRC concrete and masonry foundation walls must extend at least 6 in above the finished grade next to the foundation.
facts.note: 6 in confirmed by a 2021 IRC inspection guide. The code text also allows 4 in where masonry veneer is used (not separately confirmed).

facts.fact: Studs in exterior or bearing walls may be notched no more than 25 percent of their width; studs in nonbearing partitions up to 40 percent. Bored holes may be up to 60 percent of the stud width with the hole edge at least 5/8 in from the stud edge, but bearing-wall studs bored over 40 percent must be doubled, with no more than two successive doubled studs bored.
facts.note: Limits confirmed by Blaine MN and Scott County MN framing handouts; they are unchanged in the 2021 IRC.

facts.fact: If plumbing or ductwork requires cutting, drilling or notching more than 50 percent of the top plate width in an exterior or bearing wall, a galvanized metal tie at least 0.054 in thick (16 ga) and 1-1/2 in wide must be fastened across the cut with at least eight 10d nails on each side, extending at least 6 in past the opening.
facts.note: Confirmed by a Blaine MN framing handout; same rule in the 2021 IRC.

facts.fact: Each dwelling needs at least one egress door: a side-hinged door with a net clear width of at least 32 in (measured with the door open 90 degrees) and a clear height of at least 78 in, readily openable from inside without a key, special knowledge or effort. Other exterior doors do not have to meet these sizes.
facts.note: Confirmed by Montana DLI 2021 IRC means of egress training.

facts.fact: At the required egress door, the inside floor or landing may be no more than 1-1/2 in below the top of the threshold, and the outside landing may be up to 7-3/4 in below the threshold if the door does not swing over it. Exterior landings may slope no more than 1/4 in per foot (2 percent).
facts.note: Confirmed by Montana DLI 2021 IRC means of egress training.

facts.fact: Hallways in a dwelling must be at least 3 ft wide clear and have a ceiling height of at least 7 ft.
facts.note: Confirmed by Montana DLI 2021 IRC training and an ICC inspection guide sample.

facts.fact: IRC ramps may slope no more than 1 in 12 (8.33 percent), or 1 in 8 where that is technically infeasible because of site limits. Ramps need landings at least 36 in long at the top and bottom, and a handrail on at least one side when the slope is steeper than 1 in 12.
facts.note: Confirmed by Montana DLI 2021 IRC means of egress training.

facts.fact: IRC habitable rooms need glazing equal to at least 8 percent of the floor area for natural light and openable area of at least 4 percent of the floor area for natural ventilation. Artificial light averaging 6 footcandles and whole-house mechanical ventilation can be used instead.
facts.note: Confirmed by an ICC inspection guide sample (earlier edition) and unchanged in the 2021 IRC; the 2021 IRC mechanical ventilation reference is Section M1505.

facts.fact: A bathroom needs at least 3 sq ft of glazing, half of it openable, unless it has artificial light and a local exhaust fan of at least 50 cfm intermittent or 20 cfm continuous, vented directly to the outdoors.
facts.note: Confirmed by an ICC inspection guide sample (earlier edition, table then numbered M1507.4); same values in the 2021 IRC.

facts.fact: IRC habitable rooms (other than kitchens) must have at least 70 sq ft of floor area and be at least 7 ft in every horizontal direction. Floor area under a sloped ceiling lower than 5 ft does not count toward the required area.
facts.note: Confirmed by an ICC inspection guide sample; same in the 2021 IRC.

facts.fact: IRC ceiling heights: at least 7 ft in habitable spaces, hallways and basement areas containing them, and at least 6 ft 8 in in bathrooms, toilet rooms and laundry rooms. Beams, ducts and pipes in basements may project down to 6 ft 4 in, and a shower needs 6 ft 8 in over a 30 x 30 in area at the showerhead.
facts.note: Confirmed by an ICC inspection guide sample and Montana DLI 2021 IRC training.

facts.fact: IRC fixture clearances: at least 21 in clear in front of a water closet and lavatory, at least 15 in from the water closet centerline to a side wall or obstruction, showers at least 30 x 30 in inside, and 24 in clear in front of the shower opening.
facts.note: Confirmed by an ICC inspection guide sample; same figure in the 2021 IRC.

facts.fact: Interior stairways must be lit to at least 1 footcandle at the treads and landings, and where a stair has six or more risers a wall switch is required at each floor level unless the light is on continuously or automatically controlled.
facts.note: Confirmed by Montana DLI 2021 IRC training and an ICC inspection guide sample.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IBC, a building or tenant space used for assembly with fewer than 50 occupants is classified as Group B. An assembly room accessory to another occupancy is treated as Group B or part of the main occupancy if it has fewer than 50 occupants or is less than 750 sq ft.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 3 (2021 IBC text with marked local amendments; these sections unamended).

facts.fact: IBC assembly subgroups: A-1 fixed-seat performance spaces (theaters, concert halls); A-2 food and drink (restaurants, bars, banquet halls); A-3 worship, recreation and similar (churches, libraries, museums, gyms without spectator seating); A-4 indoor sporting events with spectator seating (arenas, indoor pools, rinks); A-5 outdoor viewing (stadiums, grandstands, bleachers).
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 3 (2021 IBC base).

facts.fact: Under the IBC, Group E covers educational use by six or more people at one time through the 12th grade, plus day care for more than five children older than 2-1/2 years for less than 24 hours a day. Training and education above the 12th grade (colleges, tutoring) is Group B, along with offices, banks and outpatient clinics.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 3 (2021 IBC base).

facts.fact: IBC residential groups: R-1 is transient lodging (hotels, motels); R-2 has more than two dwelling units or permanent sleeping units (apartments, dormitories); R-3 covers buildings with no more than two dwelling units and other small residential uses; R-4 is supervised custodial care for more than 5 but not more than 16 residents. Custodial care for more than 16 residents is Group I-1.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 3 (2021 IBC base).

facts.fact: Under the IBC, F-1 and S-1 are moderate-hazard factory and storage uses (furniture, lumber, repair garages), while F-2 and S-2 are low-hazard uses involving noncombustible materials (metal fabrication, glass, frozen foods, parking garages). Group U covers accessory structures such as private garages, carports, sheds, barns and fences over 7 ft tall.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 3 (2021 IBC base).

facts.fact: IBC Table 601 for Type I construction: Type IA needs 3-hour primary structural frame and bearing walls, 2-hour floors and 1-1/2-hour roof construction; Type IB needs 2-hour frame and bearing walls, 2-hour floors and 1-hour roof construction.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 6 (Table 601 unamended).

facts.fact: IBC Table 601: Types IIA, IIIA and VA ('A' or protected types) need 1-hour structural frame, floors and roof construction, while Types IIB and VB need no rating. Types IIIA and IIIB both require 2-hour exterior bearing walls, and Type IV-HT uses heavy timber sizes with 2-hour exterior bearing walls.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 6 (Table 601 unamended).

facts.fact: IBC 2021 occupant load factors (sq ft per person): business 150 gross, mercantile 60 gross, residential 200 gross, industrial 100 gross, warehouses 500 gross, and accessory storage or mechanical rooms 300 gross. Divide the floor area by the factor and round up.
facts.note: Confirmed in WAC 51-50-1004 (Washington's adoption of the 2021 IBC). The business factor was 100 gross before the 2018 IBC.

facts.fact: IBC 2021 occupant load factors for assembly without fixed seats: 7 net sq ft per person for concentrated use (chairs only), 5 net for standing space, and 15 net for unconcentrated use (tables and chairs). Classrooms use 20 net, vocational shops 50 net, exercise rooms 50 gross and day care 35 net.
facts.note: Confirmed in WAC 51-50-1004 (Washington's adoption of the 2021 IBC).

facts.fact: IBC 2021 maximum exit access travel distance: Groups A, E, F-1, M, R and S-1 are 200 ft without sprinklers and 250 ft with sprinklers; Group B is 200 ft without and 300 ft with sprinklers; Groups F-2, S-2 and U are 300 ft without and 400 ft with sprinklers.
facts.note: Confirmed in WAC 51-50-10170 (Washington's adoption of the 2021 IBC).

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IBC, each story needs at least 2 exits for an occupant load of 1 to 500, 3 exits for 501 to 1,000, and 4 exits for more than 1,000.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 10 and WAC 51-50-1006.

facts.fact: A space may have just one exit or exit access doorway under the 2021 IBC only if its occupant load and common path of travel stay within Table 1006.2.1. For Groups A, E and M the limit is 49 occupants and a 75-ft common path; for Group B it is 49 occupants and 100 ft (75 ft without sprinklers when more than 30 occupants).
facts.note: Confirmed in WAC 51-50-1006 (2021 IBC table).

facts.fact: When two exits or exit access doorways are required, they must be separated by at least one-half of the maximum overall diagonal of the building or area served, or one-third of the diagonal in a building with a complete automatic sprinkler system.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 10.

facts.fact: IBC egress width capacity is 0.3 in per occupant for stairways and 0.2 in per occupant for other egress components such as doors and corridors. In buildings (other than H and I-2) with full sprinklers and an emergency voice/alarm system, the factors drop to 0.2 in and 0.15 in.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 10.

facts.fact: IBC egress doors need a clear opening width of at least 32 in and a clear height of at least 80 in. Doors must swing in the direction of egress travel when they serve a room or area with an occupant load of 50 or more, or a Group H occupancy.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 10.

facts.fact: IBC 2021 minimum corridor widths: 24 in for access to mechanical, plumbing or electrical equipment; 36 in with an occupant load under 50 or inside a dwelling unit; 72 in in Group E corridors serving 100 or more occupants; and 44 in in most other cases.
facts.note: Confirmed by Building Code Trainer (2021 IBC Table 1020.3) and the CBC Table 1020.3 text.

facts.fact: Dead-end corridors are limited to 20 ft under the IBC. The limit is 50 ft in fully sprinklered Group B, E, F, I-1, M, R-1, R-2, R-4, S and U buildings, and there is no limit when the dead end is shorter than 2.5 times its least width.
facts.note: Confirmed by the CBC 1020.5 text (based on the IBC) and consistent with the 2021 IBC.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IBC, Group A-2 needs sprinklers when the fire area exceeds 5,000 sq ft, the occupant load is 100 or more, or the fire area is on a floor other than the exit discharge level. Groups A-1, A-3 and A-4 use 12,000 sq ft or an occupant load of 300 or more.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 9 (model triggers shown).

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IBC, buildings with Group F-1, M or S-1 occupancies need sprinklers throughout when the fire area exceeds 12,000 sq ft, the fire area is more than three stories above grade plane, or the combined fire area on all floors exceeds 24,000 sq ft.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 9 (model triggers).

facts.fact: The IBC requires an automatic sprinkler system throughout every building that contains a Group R fire area, which includes apartments (R-2) and hotels (R-1).
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 9.

facts.fact: The model 2021 IBC requires sprinklers in Group E when the fire area exceeds 12,000 sq ft, the occupant load is 300 or more, or the Group E fire area is on a floor other than a level of exit discharge.
facts.note: Model text confirmed from the struck-through model language in the 2021 Seattle Building Code (Washington amends this to 51 occupants).

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IBC, enclosed parking garages need sprinklers when the fire area exceeds 12,000 sq ft or the garage is under another occupancy (except R-3), and open parking garages when the fire area exceeds 48,000 sq ft. Any building with a story holding 30 or more occupants located 55 ft or more above the lowest fire department vehicle access needs sprinklers throughout.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 9.

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IBC, a manual fire alarm system is required in Group A when the occupant load is 300 or more (or more than 100 above or below the lowest exit discharge level), and in Group B when the combined occupant load of all floors is 500 or more (or more than 100 above or below the lowest exit discharge level).
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 9. Sprinklered buildings can be exempt when waterflow activates the notification appliances.

facts.fact: An accessible route must have a continuous clear width of at least 36 in. It may narrow to 32 in at points such as doorways, but only for a length of 24 in or less.
facts.note: Confirmed by the U.S. Access Board guide to ADA Standards Chapter 4 (accessible routes).

facts.fact: Where an accessible route is less than 60 in wide, passing spaces at least 60 x 60 in (or a T-shaped space with 48-in arms) are required at intervals of no more than 200 ft.
facts.note: Confirmed by the U.S. Access Board guide to ADA Standards Chapter 4.

facts.fact: A wheelchair turning space is either a 60-in diameter circle or a T-shaped space within a 60-in square with arms and base at least 36 in wide. A clear floor space for one stationary wheelchair is at least 30 x 48 in, for either a forward or a parallel approach.
facts.note: Confirmed by the U.S. Access Board guide to ADA Standards Chapter 3 (clear floor space and turning space).

facts.fact: Accessible operable parts (switches, controls, dispensers) must be within an unobstructed reach range of 15 in minimum to 48 in maximum above the floor, for both forward and side reach. Reaching over an obstruction lowers the maximum, for example to 44 in for a forward reach more than 20 in deep.
facts.note: Confirmed by the U.S. Access Board guide to ADA Standards Chapter 3 (operable parts).

facts.fact: Accessible ramp runs must be at least 36 in clear between handrails. Ramp landings must be at least as wide as the ramp run and at least 60 in long, and a landing where the ramp changes direction must be at least 60 x 60 in.
facts.note: Confirmed by the U.S. Access Board guide to ADA Standards Chapter 4 (ramps and curb ramps).

facts.fact: Curb ramps may have a running slope of no more than 1:12, flared sides no steeper than 1:10, and a top landing at least 36 in deep.
facts.note: Confirmed by the U.S. Access Board guide to ADA Standards Chapter 4 (ramps and curb ramps).

facts.fact: Minimum accessible parking spaces under the ADA: 1 for 1-25 total spaces, 2 for 26-50, 3 for 51-75, 4 for 76-100, 5 for 101-150, 6 for 151-200, 7 for 201-300, 8 for 301-400, 9 for 401-500, 2 percent of the total for 501-1,000, and 20 plus 1 per 100 over 1,000.
facts.note: Confirmed by ADA.gov parking guidance (2010 ADA Standards).

facts.fact: At least one of every six accessible parking spaces (or fraction of six) must be van accessible. Van spaces, their access aisles and the vehicle route to them need at least 98 in of vertical clearance.
facts.note: Confirmed by ADA.gov parking guidance (2010 ADA Standards).

facts.fact: In the slump test (ASTM C143), the cone is filled in three layers and each layer is rodded 25 times. The cone is then lifted straight up about 12 in in 5 seconds (plus or minus 2), the whole test must be finished within 2-1/2 minutes, and slump is reported to the nearest 1/4 in.
facts.note: Confirmed by the FDOT ASTM C143 procedure checklist.

facts.fact: Under ACI 318, one strength test is the average strength of at least two 6 x 12 in cylinders or at least three 4 x 8 in cylinders made from the same sample, normally tested at 28 days unless the construction documents say otherwise.
facts.note: Confirmed by the ACI FAQ on strength testing and NRMCA CIP 9.

facts.fact: Concrete strength is acceptable under ACI 318 when every average of three consecutive strength tests equals or exceeds the specified strength (f'c), and no single test falls more than 500 psi below f'c when f'c is 5,000 psi or less (or more than 10 percent below f'c when f'c is over 5,000 psi).
facts.note: Confirmed by the ACI FAQ (citing ACI 318-19 26.12.3.1) and NRMCA CIP 9.

facts.fact: ACI 318 strength tests for each concrete mix are taken at least once a day, at least once for every 150 cubic yards placed, and at least once for every 5,000 sq ft of slab or wall surface placed. If a mix totals less than 50 cubic yards, the building official may waive testing.
facts.note: Confirmed by West Valley City UT building department concrete testing page; consistent with ACI 318-19 26.12.2.1.

facts.source: ASTM C94 (earlier editions); California HCAI PIN 82
facts.fact: The traditional ready-mix rule is that concrete must be fully discharged within 1-1/2 hours after water is added or before the drum turns 300 revolutions, whichever comes first. Current ASTM C94 no longer sets these numbers, so the limits now come from the project specifications or the governing agency.
facts.note: Confirmed by California HCAI Policy Intent Notice 82, which notes ASTM C94 dropped the values.

facts.fact: ASTM C270 mortar types and minimum 28-day compressive strengths: Type M 2,500 psi, Type S 1,800 psi, Type N 750 psi and Type O 350 psi. The letters come from the word MaSoNwOrK, in order from strongest to weakest.
facts.note: Confirmed by Quikrete mortar specification guide (M, S, N) and Archtoolbox (all four types).

facts.source: ASTM C270 guidance; BIA Technical Note 8
facts.fact: Typical mortar uses: Type M for below-grade work with heavy loads such as foundations and retaining walls; Type S for below-grade work and where higher flexural bond is needed; Type N for general above-grade exterior and interior work; and Type O for interior non-load-bearing work and some repointing. Standard mortar joints are 3/8 in thick.
facts.note: Confirmed by Archtoolbox mortar guide and Quikrete specification guide.

facts.fact: Where Table R301.2 shows a history of ice dams at the eaves, the IRC requires an ice barrier of at least two layers of underlayment cemented together or a self-adhering polymer-modified bitumen sheet. It runs from the lowest roof edge to at least 24 in inside the exterior wall line, and on roofs sloped 8:12 or steeper it must also extend at least 36 in up the slope from the eave.
facts.note: Confirmed by City of Bozeman MT 2021 IRC roofing handout and a Grinnell IA (2015 IRC) letter.

facts.fact: Asphalt shingles may be used only on roof slopes of 2:12 or steeper. On slopes from 2:12 up to less than 4:12, a double layer of underlayment is required.
facts.note: Confirmed by Grinnell IA and Goodhue County MN IRC handouts; unchanged in the 2021 IRC.

facts.fact: IRC asphalt shingles need at least the manufacturer's number of fasteners, but never fewer than four per strip shingle or two per individual shingle. Roofing nails need at least a 12-gage shank and 3/8-in head and must go at least 3/4 in into the sheathing, or through it if the sheathing is thinner.
facts.note: Nail specs confirmed by Bozeman MT 2021 IRC handout; fastener count confirmed by an LSU AgCenter IRC roofing guide (earlier edition, same rule).

facts.fact: Under the 2021 IRC, a roof replacement must remove all existing layers of roof covering down to the roof deck. An existing self-adhered ice barrier membrane may be left in place and covered with a new ice barrier layer.
facts.note: Confirmed by City of Bozeman MT 2021 IRC roofing handout.

facts.fact: A roof recover (new roofing over an old roof) is not allowed when the existing roof is water-soaked or deteriorated, is slate, clay, cement or asbestos-cement tile, or already has two or more layers of roof covering.
facts.note: Taken from the IRC R908.3.1.1 text as commonly published; could not reach the 2021 code text to confirm wording.

facts.fact: Roofing is sold and estimated by the square: 1 square covers 100 sq ft of roof. Roof area equals plan (horizontal) area times a slope factor equal to the rafter length per foot of run; for a 6:12 roof the factor is the square root of (6x6 + 12x12) divided by 12, or about 1.118.
facts.note: Standard trade definition and geometry (Pythagorean theorem); no code citation needed.

facts.fact: For 1/2-in or 5/8-in gypsum board under the IRC, maximum fastener spacing is 7 in for nails and 12 in for screws on ceilings, and 8 in for nails on walls. Wall screws may be 16 in apart when framing is 16 in on center, but 12 in when framing is 24 in on center.
facts.note: Confirmed by City of Richland WA drywall handout reproducing Table R702.3.5.

facts.fact: Under the IRC, 1/2-in gypsum board on ceilings may span framing at 24 in on center only when installed perpendicular to the framing (16 in on center either direction), and 3/8-in board should not be used on ceilings that get a water-based texture.
facts.note: Confirmed by City of Richland WA handout reproducing Table R702.3.5 and its footnote d.

facts.fact: The 5/8-in Type X gypsum board required on a garage ceiling below habitable rooms is installed perpendicular to framing spaced up to 24 in on center, with nails or drywall screws at 6 in on center (1-7/8 in 6d coated nails or equivalent screws).
facts.note: Confirmed by City of Richland WA handout reproducing Table R702.3.5.

facts.source: FEMA/USFA engineer and architect scales guide
facts.fact: An architect's scale reads in fractions of an inch per foot (such as 1/8, 1/4, 1/2 or 1-1/2 in = 1 ft) and is used for building plans, elevations and details. An engineer's scale reads in feet per inch (1 in = 10, 20, 30, 40, 50 or 60 ft) and is used for site, road, utility and topographic drawings.
facts.note: Confirmed by the U.S. Fire Administration (FEMA) engineer/architect scales handout.

facts.source: U.S. National CAD Standard (Uniform Drawing System) sheet identification
facts.fact: Under the U.S. National CAD Standard, a sheet number like A-201 means discipline (A = architectural), sheet type (2 = elevations) and sequence (01). Common discipline letters are G general, C civil, L landscape, S structural, A architectural, P plumbing, M mechanical, E electrical and F fire protection; sheet types are 0 general, 1 plans, 2 elevations, 3 sections, 4 large-scale views, 5 details and 6 schedules and diagrams.
facts.note: Confirmed by Archtoolbox's summary of the U.S. National CAD Standard; firms may vary.

facts.source: Standard construction drawing conventions (U.S. National CAD Standard symbols)
facts.fact: On construction drawings, a section or detail callout bubble shows the drawing number on top and the sheet number where that drawing appears on the bottom; for example, 3 over A-501 means detail 3 on sheet A-501. The arrow or flag on a section cut shows the direction you are looking.
facts.note: Common drafting convention; individual offices sometimes arrange callouts differently, so check the sheet legend.

facts.source: BIA Technical Note 10 (Dimensioning and Estimating Brick Masonry)
facts.fact: A modular brick is specified as 3-5/8 x 2-1/4 x 7-5/8 in (nominal 4 x 2-2/3 x 8 in). Three courses equal 8 in of height, and a wall of modular brick takes about 6.75 brick per sq ft (675 per 100 sq ft) with 3/8-in joints, plus about 5.5 cu ft of mortar per 100 sq ft before waste.
facts.note: Confirmed in Brick Industry Association Technical Note 10. BIA suggests adding 15-25 percent for mortar waste.

facts.source: Concrete masonry nominal dimensions (8 x 8 x 16 CMU)
facts.fact: A standard 8 x 8 x 16 concrete block has a nominal face of 8 x 16 in (actual 7-5/8 x 15-5/8 in plus a 3/8-in joint), which is 0.889 sq ft, so a wall needs 1.125 blocks per sq ft (112.5 per 100 sq ft) before waste.
facts.note: Arithmetic from standard nominal CMU dimensions (128 sq in per unit).

facts.fact: Reinforcing bar weights for estimating: #3 = 0.376 lb/ft, #4 = 0.668 lb/ft, #5 = 1.043 lb/ft, #6 = 1.502 lb/ft, #7 = 2.044 lb/ft and #8 = 2.670 lb/ft. Rebar is priced by weight, so multiply total length by the weight per foot.
facts.note: Confirmed by Engineering ToolBox rebar table; these are the ASTM A615 nominal weights.

facts.source: CSI MasterFormat (2018 edition and later) division titles
facts.fact: Common MasterFormat divisions: 01 General Requirements, 02 Existing Conditions, 03 Concrete, 04 Masonry, 05 Metals, 06 Wood, Plastics and Composites, 07 Thermal and Moisture Protection, 08 Openings, 09 Finishes, 10 Specialties, 14 Conveying Equipment, 21 Fire Suppression, 22 Plumbing, 23 HVAC, 26 Electrical and 31 Earthwork.
facts.note: Confirmed by Archtoolbox's MasterFormat division list (current as of 2020).

facts.fact: IBC fire walls must be 3-hour rated for Groups A, B, E, H-4, I, R-1, R-2 and U (2 hours where separating buildings of Type II or V construction) and for F-1, H-3, H-5, M and S-1; 4-hour for H-1 and H-2; and 2-hour for F-2, S-2, R-3 and R-4. Fire walls generally run from the foundation to at least 30 in above both adjacent roofs.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 7 (Washington amends footnote a to cover Types II, III, IV and V).

facts.fact: Fire door ratings for openings (IBC Table 716.1(2)): 3-hour doors in 3- and 4-hour fire walls and fire barriers; 1-1/2-hour doors in 2-hour walls; 1-hour doors in 1-hour shaft, exit stair and exit passageway walls; 3/4-hour doors in other 1-hour fire barriers; and 20-minute doors in corridor walls and smoke barriers.
facts.note: Confirmed against the 2018 IBC Table 716.1(2) reproduced by SAFTI; the 2021 table keeps these ratings.

facts.fact: Openings in IBC fire walls and fire barriers are limited to 156 sq ft each, and their total width may not exceed 25 percent of the wall length. Fire barrier openings have exceptions for sprinklered areas and for opening protectives tested to the full wall rating.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 7.

facts.fact: In the IBC height and area tables, a full NFPA 13 sprinkler system generally adds 20 ft of height and one story. For example, a Group B building of Type VB construction is limited to 40 ft, 2 stories and 9,000 sq ft per story without sprinklers, and 60 ft, 3 stories and 27,000 sq ft per story (36,000 sq ft for a one-story building) with sprinklers.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 5 tables (B/VB row).

facts.fact: The IBC allows a frontage increase in allowable area when at least 25 percent of the building perimeter faces a public way or open space at least 20 ft wide; the increase factor grows with the percent of perimeter and the width of the open space.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 5.

facts.fact: Under the model 2021 IBC, the total area of mezzanines in a room may not exceed one-third of that room's floor area (two-thirds in certain special industrial buildings of Type I or II construction), and mezzanines need at least 7 ft of clear height.
facts.note: Model one-third limit confirmed from the struck model text in the 2021 Seattle Building Code, which amends it to one-half locally.

facts.fact: The IBC handles mixed occupancies three ways: accessory occupancies (together no more than 10 percent of the story area, usually no separation), nonseparated occupancies (the most restrictive rules apply to the whole area), or separated occupancies (fire barriers per Table 508.4, with the sum of actual-to-allowable area ratios on each story not over 1).
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 5.

facts.fact: When fire barriers are used to create separate fire areas (for example to stay under a sprinkler threshold), the IBC requires 2-hour barriers for most groups (A, B, E, F-2, I, M, R, S-2), 3-hour for F-1, H-3 and S-1, 4-hour for H-1 and H-2, and 1-hour for Group U.
facts.note: Confirmed in the 2021 Seattle Building Code Chapter 7.

facts.fact: On federal construction contracts over $35,000 but not over $150,000 (below the Miller Act bond threshold), the contracting officer must require two or more payment protections, such as a payment bond, an irrevocable letter of credit, a tripartite escrow agreement, certificates of deposit, or a deposit of approved securities.
facts.note: Confirmed on acquisition.gov (FAR 28.102-1, current version).

facts.fact: Under the Miller Act, a subcontractor or supplier who has not been paid in full within 90 days after the last day it performed labor or furnished material may sue on the prime contractor's payment bond for the unpaid amount.
facts.note: Confirmed against the statute text (Cornell LII, 40 U.S.C. 3133).

facts.fact: A Miller Act claimant who contracted with a subcontractor but not with the prime contractor (a second-tier sub or supplier) must give the prime contractor written notice of the claim within 90 days after its last labor or material, using a method that gives third-party proof of delivery. Only first-tier and second-tier claimants are protected by the bond.
facts.note: Notice rule confirmed against the statute text (Cornell LII). The statute gives rights only to those with a direct contract with the prime or with a subcontractor.

facts.fact: A Miller Act payment bond lawsuit must be filed no later than one year after the claimant's last labor or material, in the name of the United States, in the federal district court for the district where the contract was performed.
facts.note: Confirmed against the statute text (Cornell LII, 40 U.S.C. 3133).

facts.fact: On federal fixed-price construction contracts, the contracting officer must pay progress payments in full when progress is satisfactory. Retainage of up to 10 percent of a payment may be withheld only when satisfactory progress has not been made.
facts.note: Confirmed on acquisition.gov (FAR 52.232-5).

facts.fact: With each progress payment request on a federal fixed-price construction contract, the prime contractor must certify that subcontractors and suppliers have been paid from previous payments and will be paid on time from this one; without the certification, no payment is made.
facts.note: Confirmed on acquisition.gov (FAR 52.232-5).

facts.fact: A constructive change happens when the owner's representative orders extra or different work without a formal change order. Under the federal Changes clause, any written or oral order from the contracting officer that causes a change is treated as a change order if the contractor gives written notice stating the date, circumstances and source of the order and that it considers it a change.
facts.note: Confirmed on acquisition.gov (FAR 52.243-4).

facts.fact: Under the federal Changes clause, the contractor cannot recover costs incurred more than 20 days before it gives written notice of a constructive change (defective specifications are an exception), and it must assert its right to an adjustment within 30 days after receiving a written change order or giving its notice.
facts.note: Confirmed on acquisition.gov (FAR 52.243-4).

facts.fact: Federal contracts recognize two kinds of differing site conditions: Type I, subsurface or hidden conditions that differ materially from what the contract shows, and Type II, unknown unusual conditions that differ materially from what is normally found in that kind of work. The contractor must give written notice promptly and before disturbing the conditions, or the claim may be denied.
facts.note: Confirmed on acquisition.gov (FAR 52.236-2).

facts.fact: AIA contract documents are grouped by letter: A-series are owner/contractor agreements, B-series owner/architect agreements, C-series other agreements, D-series miscellaneous documents, E-series exhibits, and G-series contract administration and project management forms.
facts.note: Confirmed on AIA Contract Documents' list of current documents.

facts.fact: Key AIA documents: A101 is the owner-contractor agreement for a stipulated sum; A102 is cost of the work plus a fee with a guaranteed maximum price; A103 is cost plus a fee without a GMP; A201 is the General Conditions of the Contract for Construction; A312 is the performance bond and payment bond; and B101 is the standard owner-architect agreement.
facts.note: Titles confirmed on AIA Contract Documents' list of current documents.

facts.fact: Common AIA G-series forms: G701 change order, G704 certificate of substantial completion, G706 contractor's affidavit of payment of debts and claims, G706A affidavit of release of liens, G707 consent of surety to final payment, G710 architect's supplemental instructions, G714 construction change directive, and G716 request for information.
facts.note: Confirmed on AIA Contract Documents' G-series page.

facts.fact: Under AIA A201-2017, if the architect does not issue a certificate for payment within seven days after receiving the application (through no fault of the contractor), or the owner does not pay within seven days after the payment due date, the contractor may stop work after giving seven additional days' written notice. Contract time and sum are then adjusted for reasonable shutdown, delay and start-up costs.
facts.note: Confirmed by AIA Contract Documents article quoting Section 9.7.

facts.fact: Under AIA A201-2017, when the contractor finds concealed or unknown site conditions that differ materially from the contract documents or from what is normally found, it must notify the owner and architect promptly, before the conditions are disturbed, and no later than 14 days after first observing them.
facts.note: 14-day language confirmed in a public project copy of A201-2017 (State of Tennessee version).

facts.fact: Under AIA A201-2017, a claim must be started by written notice within 21 days after the event giving rise to it, or within 21 days after the claimant first recognizes the condition, whichever is later.
facts.note: Confirmed by a construction claims presentation summarizing A201-2017 Article 15; matches the A201 text.

facts.fact: AIA A201-2017 contains a mutual waiver of consequential damages: the owner and contractor waive claims against each other for consequential damages such as the owner's lost rental income and the contractor's home office overhead and lost profit. The waiver does not prevent the owner from assessing liquidated damages.
facts.note: Confirmed by AIA Contract Documents article quoting Section 15.1.7.

facts.source: Cal. Civ. Code 8132, 8134, 8136, 8138 (statutory lien waiver forms)
facts.fact: Lien waivers come in four basic types: conditional progress, unconditional progress, conditional final and unconditional final. California's statutory forms are a common model: a progress waiver covers work through a stated date, a final waiver covers the whole job, a conditional waiver works only if the payment is actually received, and an unconditional waiver is signed after the claimant has been paid.
facts.note: Confirmed on the California CSLB waiver and release forms page. Forms and rules vary by state; many states have no required form.

facts.fact: A conditional final lien waiver binds the claimant only when there is proof of payment, such as the claimant's endorsed check that the bank has paid. Getting a lien release from the general contractor does not by itself prove that its subcontractors and suppliers were paid.
facts.note: Confirmed on the California CSLB waiver and release forms page (California rule; other states differ).

facts.fact: Under the FLSA, employers must keep payroll records for at least 3 years, and supplementary records that wages are figured from (time cards, wage rate tables, work schedules, records of additions and deductions) for 2 years.
facts.note: Confirmed by DOL Wage and Hour Fact Sheet #21.

facts.source: 29 CFR Part 785; DOL WHD Fact Sheet #22
facts.fact: Under the FLSA, a normal home-to-work commute is not work time, but travel from job site to job site during the workday is paid work time. Short rest breaks (usually 20 minutes or less) must be counted as hours worked, and on-call time spent on the employer's premises is work time.
facts.note: Confirmed by DOL Wage and Hour Fact Sheet #22.

facts.source: 29 CFR 541.600; DOL final rule issued May 15, 2026
facts.fact: To be exempt from FLSA overtime as an executive, administrative or professional employee, a worker must pass the duties test and be paid a salary of at least $684 per week ($35,568 a year); the highly compensated employee threshold is $107,432 a year. A 2026 DOL rule rescinded the 2024 increases and kept these 2019 levels.
facts.note: Confirmed by L&E Global summary of the May 2026 DOL final rule. Some states set higher salary thresholds.

facts.fact: An employer enrolled in E-Verify must complete Form I-9 first and then create the E-Verify case no later than the third business day after the new employee starts work for pay.
facts.note: Confirmed on e-verify.gov (User Manual section 2.2).

facts.fact: When E-Verify returns a mismatch (tentative nonconfirmation) and the employee chooses to take action, the employee has 8 federal government working days to contact SSA or DHS. The employer may not fire, suspend or take other adverse action because of the mismatch while it is being resolved.
facts.note: Confirmed on e-verify.gov.

facts.source: DOL WHD proposed rule (Feb. 26, 2026); Field Assistance Bulletin 2025-1
facts.fact: Under the FLSA, worker status is decided by an 'economic reality' test that asks whether the worker is really in business for themselves. The two core factors are the business's control over the work and the worker's opportunity for profit or loss; skill, permanence and whether the work is part of an integrated unit also count, and actual practice matters more than the contract wording.
facts.note: Confirmed by DLA Piper summary of DOL's 2026 proposed rule and 2025 enforcement guidance. The federal rule is in flux, and some states (such as California's ABC test) are stricter.

facts.source: EEOC coverage of private employers; 42 U.S.C. 2000e(b)
facts.fact: Title VII, the ADA and GINA cover private employers with 15 or more employees, and the Age Discrimination in Employment Act covers employers with 20 or more, counting employees who worked at least 20 calendar weeks in the current or preceding year. The Equal Pay Act covers virtually all employers.
facts.note: Confirmed on the EEOC coverage page for private employers.

facts.fact: The Age Discrimination in Employment Act protects workers who are at least 40 years old.
facts.note: Confirmed against the statute text (Cornell LII).

facts.source: EEOC: Time Limits for Filing a Charge
facts.fact: A discrimination charge generally must be filed with the EEOC within 180 calendar days of the discrimination, extended to 300 days where a state or local agency enforces a law against the same discrimination. Equal Pay Act claims can go straight to court within 2 years of the last discriminatory paycheck (3 years if willful).
facts.note: Confirmed on eeoc.gov. For age claims, only a state law (not a local one) extends the deadline to 300 days.

facts.fact: The annual EEO-1 report of workforce demographics is required of private employers with 100 or more employees and of federal contractors with 50 or more employees that meet certain criteria.
facts.note: Confirmed on eeoc.gov EEO data collections page.

facts.source: IRS Employment Tax Due Dates; Form 941 instructions
facts.fact: Form 941 is due by the last day of the month after each quarter: April 30, July 31, October 31 and January 31. An employer that deposited all its taxes on time gets 10 more calendar days to file.
facts.note: Confirmed on irs.gov Employment Tax Due Dates page.

facts.source: IRS Employment Tax Due Dates; IRS Pub 15
facts.fact: Monthly depositors deposit a month's employment taxes by the 15th of the following month. Semiweekly depositors deposit taxes on Wednesday, Thursday or Friday paydays by the following Wednesday, and on Saturday through Tuesday paydays by the following Friday.
facts.note: Confirmed on irs.gov Employment Tax Due Dates page.

facts.source: IRS Backup Withholding; Form W-9; Employment Tax Due Dates
facts.fact: Before paying a subcontractor, get a signed Form W-9 with its taxpayer identification number. If a payee does not provide a correct TIN, the payer must apply backup withholding at 24 percent. Form 1099-NEC is due to both the recipient and the IRS by January 31.
facts.note: Confirmed on irs.gov backup withholding and employment tax due dates pages.

facts.fact: Withheld income tax and the employee's share of Social Security and Medicare are 'trust fund' taxes. Any responsible person (such as an owner, officer or bookkeeper with authority) who willfully fails to collect or pay them over can be held personally liable for a Trust Fund Recovery Penalty equal to the full unpaid trust fund amount.
facts.note: Confirmed in the IRS Internal Revenue Manual 8.25.1.

facts.fact: Under MACRS, automobiles and light general-purpose trucks are 5-year property, office furniture and equipment are 7-year property, residential rental buildings (80 percent or more of rent from dwelling units) are 27.5-year property, and nonresidential real property is 39-year property. Land is never depreciated.
facts.note: Confirmed in IRS Form 4562 instructions and IRS Pub 946 (land).

facts.fact: MACRS normally uses the half-year convention, which treats property as placed in service in the middle of the year. The mid-quarter convention applies instead when more than 40 percent of the year's depreciable property is placed in service in the last 3 months of the tax year.
facts.note: Confirmed in IRS Form 4562 instructions.

facts.source: IRC 179; IRS Pub 946 (2026 limits); One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)
facts.fact: Section 179 lets a business expense the cost of qualifying equipment in the year it is placed in service. For tax years beginning in 2026 the limit is $2,560,000, reduced dollar for dollar once qualifying property placed in service exceeds $4,090,000 (the 2025 figures were $2.5 million and $4 million).
facts.note: 2026 figures confirmed in IRS Pub 946; 2025 figures confirmed by Sikich summary of the 2025 law. Limits are indexed for inflation each year.

facts.source: IRC 168(k) as amended by the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025)
facts.fact: Bonus depreciation is permanently set at 100 percent for qualifying property acquired after January 19, 2025, so the full cost of eligible equipment can be deducted in the first year. Property acquired earlier (based on the written binding contract date) gets the lower phase-down rate.
facts.note: Confirmed by Sikich summary of the 2025 law.

facts.fact: Debt-to-equity ratio = total liabilities divided by owner's equity. A contractor with $300,000 of liabilities and $200,000 of equity has a ratio of 1.5, meaning creditors have put in $1.50 for every $1 the owners have; sureties and lenders prefer lower ratios.
facts.note: Standard accounting formula (consistent with the debt ratio and accounting equation facts already in the knowledge base).

facts.source: Percentage-of-completion (cost-to-cost) method; construction WIP schedule practice
facts.fact: On a work-in-progress (WIP) schedule, percent complete = costs to date divided by total estimated costs, and earned revenue = percent complete times the contract value. Example: $750,000 of cost on a job estimated at $1,000,000 is 75 percent complete, so on a $1,200,000 contract the earned revenue is $900,000.
facts.note: Method confirmed by Corpay's construction WIP report guide.

facts.source: Construction WIP schedule practice (balance sheet presentation)
facts.fact: If a contractor has billed more than it has earned, the overbilling is a current liability called 'billings in excess of costs and estimated earnings.' If it has earned more than it has billed, the underbilling is a current asset called 'costs and estimated earnings in excess of billings.'
facts.note: Confirmed by Corpay's construction WIP report guide.

facts.fact: A work-related injury or illness is recordable on the OSHA 300 log if it results in death, days away from work, restricted work or job transfer, medical treatment beyond first aid, or loss of consciousness, or if it is a significant injury or illness diagnosed by a physician or other licensed health care professional.
facts.note: Confirmed on eCFR (29 CFR 1904.7).

facts.fact: OSHA's list of first aid treatments is complete; anything not on it is medical treatment. First aid includes nonprescription medicine at nonprescription strength, tetanus shots, cleaning wounds, bandages, hot or cold therapy, non-rigid supports like elastic wraps, temporary splints for transport, eye patches, removing splinters by simple means, and drinking fluids for heat stress.
facts.note: Confirmed on eCFR (29 CFR 1904.7).

facts.fact: When counting days away from work or restricted days for the OSHA 300 log, start counting the day after the injury, count calendar days (not just scheduled workdays), and stop at 180 days.
facts.note: Confirmed on eCFR (29 CFR 1904.7).

facts.fact: The annual OSHA 300A summary must be certified by a company executive: an owner (sole proprietorship or partnership only), a corporate officer, the highest-ranking company official at the establishment, or that official's immediate supervisor.
facts.note: Confirmed on eCFR (29 CFR 1904.32).

facts.source: 29 CFR 1904.41; Appendices A and B to Subpart E
facts.fact: Construction establishments with 20 to 249 employees (and all record-keeping establishments with 250 or more) must submit their OSHA 300A data electronically by March 2 each year. Establishments with 100 or more employees in an Appendix B industry, which includes NAICS 2381 foundation, structure and building exterior contractors, must also submit their 300 and 301 data.
facts.note: Confirmed on eCFR (29 CFR 1904.41 and Appendices A and B; Appendix A lists NAICS 23 Construction).

facts.fact: A work-related death must be reported to OSHA only if it occurs within 30 days of the incident, and an in-patient hospitalization, amputation or loss of an eye only if it occurs within 24 hours of the incident. In-patient hospitalization means formal admission, not just observation or tests, and a motor vehicle crash on a public road is reportable only if it happened in a construction work zone.
facts.note: Confirmed on eCFR (29 CFR 1904.39).

questions.q: Under the 2021 IRC, what is the minimum clear width of a stairway above the permitted handrail height?
questions.why: R311.7.1 requires stairways to be at least 36 in clear above the handrail height; 44 in is the common IBC egress stair width.

questions.q: Under the 2021 IRC, a nosing is not required on a stair when the tread depth is at least:
questions.why: Nosings of 3/4 to 1-1/4 in are required on solid-riser stairs unless the tread depth is 11 in or more.

questions.q: Under the 2021 IRC, a guard is required where an open-sided deck is more than how high above the grade below (measured within 36 in of the edge)?
questions.why: Guards are required where the walking surface is more than 30 in above the floor or grade within 36 in horizontally of the open side.

questions.q: What is the minimum required guard height for a deck in a one-family dwelling under the model 2021 IRC?
questions.why: R312.1.2 requires 36 in guards; 34 in applies to guards along the open sides of stairs, and 42 in is the IBC (and some state) requirement.

questions.q: Guards on the open side of an IRC stairway may not have openings that pass a sphere of what diameter?
questions.why: The general guard limit is a 4 in sphere, but the open side of stairs is allowed 4-3/8 in; the 6 in sphere applies only to the riser/tread/bottom rail triangle.

questions.q: Window fall protection is required when an operable window's sill is less than 24 in above the floor and the opening is more than how high above the grade outside?
questions.why: R312.2.1 applies where the sill is under 24 in above the finished floor and the opening is more than 72 in above the grade below.

questions.q: What is the minimum net clear opening for an emergency escape window on a second-floor bedroom under the 2021 IRC?
questions.why: Escape openings need at least 5.7 sq ft; the 5.0 sq ft allowance is only for grade-floor openings.

questions.q: A window well serving a basement escape window needs a permanently attached ladder or steps when the well is deeper than:
questions.why: Area wells deeper than 44 in require a permanent ladder or steps that can be used with the window fully open.

questions.q: Which window pane requires safety glazing under IRC R308.4.3?
c: 10 sq ft pane, bottom edge 16 in above floor, top edge 70 in, walkway 24 in away
8 sq ft pane, bottom edge 12 in above floor, top edge 60 in, walkway 24 in away
12 sq ft pane, bottom edge 20 in above floor, top edge 80 in, walkway 24 in away
12 sq ft pane, bottom edge 12 in above floor, top edge 80 in, walkway 48 in away
questions.why: All four conditions must be met: over 9 sq ft, bottom under 18 in, top over 36 in, and a walking surface within 36 in. Each wrong choice misses one condition.

questions.q: What is the minimum horizontal distance between an ionization smoke alarm without a silencing switch and a permanently installed cooking appliance?
questions.why: Ionization alarms must be at least 20 ft away (10 ft with a silencing switch); photoelectric alarms need 6 ft.

questions.q: Under the 2021 IRC, which new all-electric home is required to have carbon monoxide alarms?
c: One heated by an electric heat pump
One with an attached garage that has a door into the house
questions.why: CO alarms are required where there is a fuel-fired appliance or an attached garage with an opening into the dwelling.

questions.q: Under the IRC, what must separate a garage from a habitable room located above it?
c: 1/2 in regular gypsum board on the garage side
questions.why: Table R302.6 requires at least 5/8 in Type X gypsum board between a garage and habitable rooms above; 1/2 in board is enough for walls between the garage and the house.

questions.q: A house without sprinklers has an exterior wall 4 ft from the lot line. Under Table R302.1(1), how much of that wall may be openings?
questions.why: Openings are not allowed under 3 ft, limited to 25 percent of the wall area from 3 ft to under 5 ft, and unlimited at 5 ft or more.

questions.q: What is the minimum thickness of a concrete spread footing under IRC R403.1.1?
questions.why: Footings must be at least 6 in thick and 12 in wide, with a projection of at least 2 in but not more than the footing thickness.

questions.q: A stud in an exterior bearing wall may be notched to a maximum depth of what percent of its width?
questions.why: Bearing studs may be notched 25 percent; nonbearing studs 40 percent; bored holes may be up to 60 percent of the width.

questions.q: An office floor of 15,000 gross sq ft is used as business space. What is its occupant load under 2021 IBC Table 1004.5?
questions.why: Business areas use 150 gross sq ft per occupant: 15,000 / 150 = 100 occupants.

questions.q: A banquet hall has 3,000 net sq ft set with tables and chairs. What is its occupant load?
questions.why: Unconcentrated assembly (tables and chairs) uses 15 net sq ft per person: 3,000 / 15 = 200. 429 would be the chairs-only factor of 7, and 600 the standing factor of 5.

questions.q: What is the maximum exit access travel distance in a fully sprinklered Group B building under the 2021 IBC?
questions.why: Group B allows 200 ft without sprinklers and 300 ft with sprinklers; 250 ft applies to sprinklered A, E, F-1, M, R and S-1.

questions.q: A story has an occupant load of 750. What is the minimum number of exits required from that story?
questions.why: Two exits serve 1-500 occupants, three serve 501-1,000, and four are needed above 1,000.

questions.q: What is the minimum corridor width for a corridor serving 120 occupants in an office building under the 2021 IBC?
questions.why: The general minimum is 44 in; 36 in applies only with fewer than 50 occupants, and 72 in is for Group E corridors serving 100 or more.

questions.q: Under IBC Table 601, what fire-resistance rating is required for the primary structural frame of Type IA construction?
questions.why: Type IA requires a 3-hour primary structural frame; Type IB requires 2 hours.

questions.q: Under the 2021 IBC, a Group A-2 restaurant must be sprinklered when its fire area exceeds:
questions.why: A-2 occupancies need sprinklers over 5,000 sq ft, with 100 or more occupants, or on a floor other than the exit discharge level.

questions.q: An assisted living facility provides 24-hour custodial care to 20 residents. What is its IBC occupancy classification?
questions.why: R-4 covers more than 5 but not more than 16 residents; more than 16 residents in custodial care is Group I-1.

questions.q: What minimum fire protection rating is required for a door in a 2-hour fire barrier?
questions.why: Table 716.1(2) requires 1-1/2-hour doors in 2-hour fire walls and fire barriers; 1-hour shaft and exit enclosures need 1-hour doors.

questions.q: A parking lot has 120 total spaces. How many accessible spaces does the 2010 ADA Standards require?
questions.why: 101-150 total spaces require 5 accessible spaces, and at least one of them must be van accessible.

questions.q: Under ACI 318, when f'c is 4,000 psi, no individual strength test may fall below f'c by more than:
questions.why: For f'c of 5,000 psi or less, no single test may be more than 500 psi low, and every average of three consecutive tests must reach f'c.

questions.q: Which ASTM C270 mortar type has a minimum compressive strength of 1,800 psi?
questions.why: Type M is 2,500 psi, Type S 1,800 psi, Type N 750 psi and Type O 350 psi.

questions.q: Where an ice barrier is required by the IRC, it must extend from the lowest roof edge to a point at least how far inside the exterior wall line?
questions.why: The ice barrier extends at least 24 in inside the exterior wall line; on roofs 8:12 or steeper it must also run at least 36 in up the slope.

questions.q: About how many modular brick are needed for 400 sq ft of wall with 3/8-in joints, before waste?
questions.why: Modular brick runs about 6.75 per sq ft: 400 x 6.75 = 2,700 brick.

questions.q: A roof has 2,000 sq ft of plan area and a 6:12 slope (slope factor 1.118). About how many squares of roofing does it need before waste?
questions.why: Roof area = 2,000 x 1.118 = 2,236 sq ft, and one square is 100 sq ft, so about 22.4 squares.

questions.q: Under the Miller Act, a supplier to a subcontractor must give the prime contractor written notice of its claim within how many days after its last delivery?
questions.why: Second-tier claimants must give written notice to the prime within 90 days of their last labor or material.

questions.q: What is the deadline to file a Miller Act payment bond lawsuit?
c: 90 days after last labor or material
1 year after last labor or material
questions.why: Suit must be filed no later than one year after the claimant last performed labor or supplied material, in federal district court.

questions.q: On a federal fixed-price construction contract, when may the contracting officer hold back retainage, and how much?
c: Only if progress is unsatisfactory, up to 10 percent
Only on the final payment, up to 20 percent
questions.why: FAR 52.232-5(e) requires full payment when progress is satisfactory; up to 10 percent may be retained only when it is not.

questions.q: Under the federal Changes clause, a contractor cannot recover costs of a constructive change incurred more than how many days before it gave written notice?
questions.why: Costs incurred more than 20 days before written notice are not recoverable (except for defective specifications); the 30-day rule is for asserting the adjustment.

questions.q: Which describes a Type I differing site condition?
c: Extra work ordered orally by the owner
Subsurface or hidden conditions that differ materially from those shown in the contract
Unknown unusual conditions that differ from those ordinarily encountered
questions.why: Type I is a material difference from what the contract indicates; Type II is an unusual condition that differs from what is normally encountered.

questions.q: Which AIA document is the owner-contractor agreement for the cost of the work plus a fee with a guaranteed maximum price?
questions.why: A101 is stipulated sum, A102 is cost plus fee with a GMP, A103 is cost plus fee without a GMP, and A201 is the general conditions.

questions.q: Under AIA A201-2017, if the owner fails to pay within seven days after the payment due date, the contractor may stop work after giving how many additional days' written notice?
questions.why: Section 9.7 lets the contractor stop work on seven additional days' notice and recover reasonable shutdown, delay and start-up costs.

questions.q: A subcontractor is about to receive a progress check it has not yet been paid. Which lien waiver should it sign?
questions.why: A conditional progress waiver takes effect only if the progress payment is actually received; unconditional waivers are for payments already received.

questions.q: To be exempt from overtime under the FLSA white-collar exemptions, an employee must pass the duties test and be paid a salary of at least:
questions.why: The 2026 DOL rule rescinded the 2024 increases, leaving the threshold at $684 per week ($35,568 a year).

questions.q: An employer enrolled in E-Verify must create the E-Verify case for a new hire no later than:
c: Before the job offer is made
The employee's first day of work
The third business day after the employee starts work for pay
questions.why: Form I-9 is completed first, and the E-Verify case must be created by the third business day after the employee starts work for pay.

questions.q: When is Form 941 for January through March due?
questions.why: Form 941 is due the last day of the month after the quarter ends (April 30, July 31, October 31, January 31), with 10 extra days if all deposits were on time.

questions.q: A subcontractor refuses to provide its taxpayer identification number on Form W-9. At what rate must the payer apply backup withholding?
questions.why: The current backup withholding rate is 24 percent.

questions.q: A contractor has total liabilities of $450,000 and owner's equity of $300,000. What is its debt-to-equity ratio?
questions.why: Debt-to-equity = total liabilities / owner's equity = $450,000 / $300,000 = 1.5.

questions.q: A $1,000,000 contract has $600,000 of costs to date and $800,000 of total estimated costs. Using cost-to-cost percentage of completion, what is the earned revenue?
questions.why: Percent complete = $600,000 / $800,000 = 75 percent, and 75 percent of $1,000,000 = $750,000 earned.

questions.q: A worker dies from injuries 45 days after a work-related incident. Must the employer report the death to OSHA?
c: No, a fatality is reportable only if it occurs within 30 days of the incident
No, fatalities are only recorded on the 300 log after 7 days
Yes, within 8 hours of learning of it
questions.why: Fatalities must be reported within 8 hours only if the death occurs within 30 days of the work-related incident; the case is still recorded on the 300 log.
